name: Beth Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartley Trailers, where we build horse trailers and farm trailers. I load steel parts into the jig, which is the frame that holds them in place, for a welding robot, then press start and check the welds when it's done. I've been there nine months, and I still get the clamps in the wrong order sometimes, so the robot stops and beeps at me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love watching the robot work, and I ask an AI app every day about weld settings and why a seam went porous, which means full of tiny bubbles. My partner Tom is a carpentry apprentice, so we're both on learner pay with less than a month saved. What wears me out is the early start, 6am, and the grind on the clamps in winter when the steel is freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the market decided it wasn't worth it. At work I'd say let's just build good trailers. Online I'd share something about hard work beating hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit disappointed, because I liked the idea of moving up with the tech. Without big change, I'm still on learner pay in a town with three factories. Hartley's order book depends on farmers, and farmers have had a bad couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask the supervisor, Mr Okafor, if I can learn to program the welding robot properly. I'd keep using AI to learn faster at home. And Tom and I would stick to the budget, no takeaways, to build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, but I'll get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Hartley in a bad farming year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They cut the overtime first, then the agency staff. Last spring we went to four days for a month, and I lost about a fifth of my pay. Tom's mum fed us Sundays that month, which I was grateful for and embarrassed about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why embarrassed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like standing on my own two feet. My parents never took help from anyone. But family helping family is different from handouts, I suppose.

I'd tell coworkers to just **build good trailers**.

feel: She feels **a bit flat**, but gets on with it.

steps.text: Ask Mr Okafor to teach her the welding robot's programming
Stick to a no-takeaway budget with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and the people who adapt will do well. At work I'd offer to help others with the new software. Online I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me, honestly. Hartley's office would shrink, the ordering and quoting goes to AI, but the welding robots need people who understand them. I'm already halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Mr Okafor to put me on the robot programming course. I'd ask if Hartley would pay for a welding qualification too, because a robot programmer who can weld by hand is worth more. And I'd save the overtime, not spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly confident, with a nervous edge because of the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out at Hartley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra in the office, who does the quotes for farmers over the phone. Farmers like talking to her, they trust her. I'd hope Hartley keeps her for that. An app won't know a farmer's name the way our office lady Sandra does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's good for you. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If farmers have another bad year, nobody buys trailers whatever the tech. Then it's not the robots that get me, it's the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should keep their workers and train them, not dump them. I'd post that apprenticeships are the answer, not benefits. At work I'd say keep learning, it's all we can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared. By 2028 the robot programming I'm learning is thinking work, so AI does that. By 2031 the robots load their own jigs, and I'm 31 with skills that expired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch to robot maintenance, the hands-on part, which lasts until about 2031. Tom and I would move in with my parents to save. And I'd look into the family farm, my uncle's, because people will always need food and someone to run the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually first in line for change, and even I can't find the front of this queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the farm offer you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Graham has a dairy farm and no kids who want it. I could learn to run the milking robots, which they already have. It's not glamorous, but it's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got each other and our families. We'd tighten up, live at my mum's, and keep working. My partner Tom would be fine, because he's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up, so let's be sensible. At work I'd help people learn new skills. Online I'd share stuff about trade schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me use robot programming for a few years, then move into maintenance before 2034. It's a two-step plan, and I like a plan. Tom has time to finish his apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot programming course this year, then a maintenance certificate in year three. Tom and I would save fifty a month, no holidays. And I'd keep in touch with my uncle about the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. I'd rather be busy than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the farm option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a backup. My uncle would want me trained on the milking robots first. Maybe I'd do a weekend there now and then to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've got a plan and I'm not asking for money. My dad would like that, he's proud of standing on his own. They'd help if we really needed it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready, so no excuses. At work I'd help train people. I'd post about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years lets me build a proper career and maybe take over the farm. By 2039 I'd be 40. A dairy farm with robots still needs someone in charge. I'd rather own the machines than be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn robot programming and maintenance over the next few years. Tom and I would save for a house near the farm. And I'd start helping my uncle with the business side, learning how a farm makes money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Ten years feels like a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is taking over the farm realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My uncle's 62, and he'd want it to stay in the family. We'd need a loan, but farmers get those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What if the robots don't need anyone in charge by 2039? That's the bit I can't plan for. But I'd still rather own the farm than not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my skills would expire before I could use them. What would help is businesses paying for apprenticeships and families sticking together. Not benefits, a chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farm. A lot of us young ones might end up back on family land. Someone should make that easier, not harder.

headlineQuote: A lot of us young ones might end up back on family land.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** welding robot operator at Hartley Trailers.
She uses AI **every day** and wants to move up with the tech.
She lives with Tom, a **carpentry apprentice**, on learner pay.
She sees **Steady Disruption** as an opening, but AGI by 2028 alarms her.
Her backup is her **uncle's dairy farm**, which she might take over.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, as her **skills expire** too soon.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **families** to stick together, with a chance to work.
